sentences.text: Eoalligator possessed a short, blunt snout that shared physical traits with both crocodyloids and alligatoroids.
The upper jaw displayed a pattern of alternating concave and convex regions along the tooth row, a feature known as festooning.
The front section of the lower jaw was notably short, extending only as far as the fourth tooth.
A distinct depression on the lower jaw bone represents a unique characteristic shared between Eoalligator and Asiatosuchus nanlingensis.
Scientists propose that this depression on the lower jaw might become less prominent as the animal matures.
In the front teeth, the third tooth was the largest while the fifth was the smallest.
Upper teeth were described as blunt with smooth edges, differing from the bulbous teeth seen in early Globidonta.
An early researcher named Young estimated that the lower jaw contained 23 teeth in total.
The fourth tooth in the lower jaw was likely the largest and fit into a specific socket located between the front and upper jaw bones.
The 11th and 12th teeth in the lower jaw were enlarged, though not to the same extent as the fourth tooth.
This extinct crocodilian is described as being of moderate size.
Fossils of the only known species, Eoalligator chunyii, were discovered and described in 1964 alongside the remains of Asiatosuchus nanlingensis.
The genus Eoalligator was named in 1964 by Yang Zhongjian based on fossil material collected in Guangdong Province.
The original material for Eoalligator chunyii was found in three localities within 8 km of each other in Nanxiong County.
A second species, Eoalligator huiningensis, was described in 1982 from material found in Anhui Province.
Fossils of Eoalligator have been found in multiple locations within China's Nanxiong Basin.
There are three recorded fossil occurrences of Eoalligator in the Paleobiology Database.
The classification of Eoalligator has shifted over time, moving from alligatorine to crocodyloid and finally to the clade Orientalosuchina.
A 2016 study classified Eoalligator as a member of Crocodylidae and suggested it might be the same species as Asiatosuchus nanlingensis.
A later study disagreed with the idea that Eoalligator and Asiatosuchus nanlingensis are the same species, though both agreed Eoalligator is a crocodyloid.
Eoalligator was reclassified as an alligatoroid when a new group called Orientalosuchina was established.
Recent studies place Eoalligator as the closest relative to the Cretaceous crocodilian Jiangxisuchus.
Eoalligator belongs to the parent group Orientalosuchina.
Eoalligator is classified as a reptile.
The type species of the genus Eoalligator is Eoalligator chunyii.
Eoalligator is an extinct crocodilian found in Late Cretaceous to Paleocene sediments of China.
Fossils of Eoalligator chunyii come from the Zhenshui Formation (Late Cretaceous) and the Shanghu Formation (Lower Paleocene).
Eoalligator fossils from the Shanghu Formation date to after the K-PG extinction event.
Eoalligator lived between 60.9 and 57.5 million years ago during the Selandian to Thanetian stages.
It is debated whether Eoalligator chunyii and Asiatosuchus nanlingensis represent the same animal or distinct species.
Researchers questioned the validity of Eoalligator huiningensis because the original describer did not compare it to E. chunyii and they lacked shared diagnostic traits.
A 2024 study raised doubts about whether the group Orientalosuchina, which includes Eoalligator, is truly an alligatoroid or more closely related to crocodyloids.
Researchers acknowledge that the alternative classification placing Orientalosuchina within Mekosuchinae has relatively weak support and needs more study.
